nodeData.topic: Statics: forces, free-body diagrams and equilibrium
nodeData.note: Why a bridge, a roof truss or a water-tank stand stays still: the forces and the turning effects on it add to zero. Own-words notes from OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1 (free, CC BY) sections 5.7, 12.1, 12.2; tap a bubble for the page. SI units, g = 9.8 m/s². Search words: statics, equilibrium, free body diagram, FBD, torque, moment, lever arm, reaction, tension, normal force, friction.

children.note: Equilibrium for a rigid body: zero linear acceleration and zero angular (turning) acceleration at the same time. At rest in our frame it is in static equilibrium; moving at constant velocity it is in dynamic equilibrium — the same equations apply.

manas.q: Define equilibrium of a rigid body.

children.note: A particle has no size, so only forces matter. A rigid body has size, so where a force acts matters too — that is what adds torque to the problem.
A crate at rest on a moving lorry is in static equilibrium for the driver and dynamic equilibrium for someone on the road. The laws are the same in every inertial frame.

children.topic: Newton's first law is the statics law
children.note: No net force → no change in motion. Statics is Newton's first law applied to forces and to torques.

manas.q: Which of Newton's laws does statics rest on?

children.note: Nudge it and watch. Stable: forces push it back (a marble in a bowl). Unstable: it moves further away (a marble on an upturned bowl). Neutral: it stays where you left it (a marble on a flat table). All three satisfy ΣF = 0 — only the nudge tells them apart.

manas.q: Name the three kinds of equilibrium and give an example of each.

children.note: Stable equilibrium sits at a low point of potential energy, unstable at a high point. Why: from a valley every small move goes uphill and gravity pulls it back; from a hilltop every move goes downhill.

manas.q: Is a stable equilibrium at a minimum or a maximum of potential energy?

children.topic: Lifting: hook above the centre of gravity
children.note: When a crane lifts a load, the centre of gravity should hang below the lift point; at or above it the load tends to tip over. Riggers find the centre of gravity before every lift — getting it wrong has cost lives.

children.topic: Finding the centre of gravity: hang it twice
children.note: Hang the object from one point and mark the vertical line (a plumb line) below it; hang it from another point and mark again. The lines cross at the centre of mass. Works for an odd-shaped steel plate in the workshop.

manas.q: How do you find the centre of gravity of an irregular flat plate?

children.note: Six forces cover most first-year problems. Each has a fixed direction rule — learn the rule and the diagram draws itself.

manas.q: List the common forces and the direction each one acts in.

children.note: Acts at the centre of mass. A 20 kg beam weighs 20 × 9.8 = 196 N. The only common force that needs no contact.

manas.q: What is the weight of a 60 kg person on Earth?

children.topic: Normal force N, perpendicular to the surface
children.note: The push of a surface on the body, always at right angles to the surface and away from it. On a slope it is tilted, not vertical.

children.topic: Tension T, along the rope, away from the body
children.note: A rope can only pull. The same tension acts at both ends of a light rope.

children.topic: Friction f, along the surface, opposing motion
children.note: Opposes the motion or the intended motion. Static friction can be anything up to a maximum μₛN; kinetic friction is μₖN.

manas.q: In which direction does friction act on a block held still on a slope?

children.note: A hand, a cable from a winch, a wind load — drawn at the angle the problem states.

children.topic: Spring force, towards the natural length
children.note: Proportional to the stretch or compression (Hooke's law). Pushes or pulls back towards the unstretched position.
What a support can push back with depends on how it is made. Count the unknowns a support brings before you count equations.

manas.q: How many unknowns do a roller, a pin and a fixed support each add?

children.note: One force perpendicular to the surface. It cannot pull or resist sliding.
A force of unknown size and direction — write it as two components. It cannot resist turning.
Two force components plus a moment, because the wall stops the beam turning. A cantilever balcony is this case.
Draw the body alone, with every external force on it as an arrow. Done right, the diagram is most of the solution; done wrong, no algebra can save it.

manas.q: State the four rules for a free-body diagram.

children.note: Sketch the object (a dot if treating it as a particle) with x–y axes. Circle it so you only mark forces acting ON it.

children.topic: Rule 2: all external forces, no net force
children.note: Weight, normal, tension, friction, applied, spring. Never draw the net force; never draw forces the body exerts on other things; never both halves of an action–reaction pair.

manas.q: Name two things that must never appear on a free-body diagram.

children.topic: Rule 3: replace angled forces by components
children.note: Draw the x and y components and put a squiggle through the original arrow so you do not count it twice.
Two blocks, two diagrams. Forces between them appear on both, equal and opposite.
If the body accelerates, note the acceleration beside the diagram in another colour, not as an arrow on it.
Forces: pull P at 30° above the ground, weight down, normal up, friction backwards. Components of P: P cos 30° forward, P sin 30° upward — the upward part reduces the normal force.

manas.q: A sled is pulled by 100 N at 30°. Forward and upward components?

children.note: Forward 100 × cos 30° = 86.6 N; upward 100 × sin 30° = 50 N. Check: 86.6² + 50² ≈ 100².

children.topic: Example: two blocks on an incline
children.note: Block A on top of block B on a slope: separate diagrams. Friction from B on A points one way; friction from A on B the opposite way — they are a third-law pair, equal in size.
Ask: which way would the body slide if the surface were ice? Friction points the other way.

children.topic: First condition: forces sum to zero
children.note: ΣF = 0, which in components means ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 (and ΣFz = 0 in 3-D). This alone solves particle problems — knots, hanging loads, blocks held on slopes.

manas.q: Write the first equilibrium condition in component form.

children.topic: Worked: lamp on two symmetric cables
children.note: A 5.0 kg lamp (49 N) hangs from two cables, each 30° above horizontal. Vertical: 2T sin 30° = 49, so T = 49 N. Horizontal: the two T cos 30° cancel by symmetry.

manas.q: A 5 kg lamp hangs from two cables at 30° above horizontal. Tension in each?

children.note: At 10° above horizontal: T = 49 / (2 sin 10°) = 141 N — nearly three times the lamp's weight. A perfectly horizontal cable would need infinite tension, which is why washing lines sag.

manas.q: Why can a clothes line never be pulled perfectly straight?

children.topic: Worked: block held on a 30° slope
children.note: 10 kg block at rest on a 30° incline. Along the slope: friction f = mg sin 30° = 98 × 0.5 = 49 N, up the slope. Perpendicular: N = mg cos 30° = 84.9 N.

manas.q: A 10 kg block rests on a 30° slope: find the friction and normal force.

children.note: μ must be at least f/N = 49/84.9 = 0.58 = tan 30°. In general a block stays put while tan θ ≤ μₛ.

children.topic: Choose axes to suit the problem
children.note: On a slope, take x along the slope and y perpendicular to it; then N has no x-component and only weight needs splitting.
Στ = 0: the turning effects about any axis also cancel. Needed whenever the body has size — beams, ladders, seesaws, cranes, bridge decks.

manas.q: Write the second equilibrium condition and say when it is needed.

children.note: τ = r F sin θ: the force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action. Unit N·m (not joules, though the base units match).

manas.q: A 200 N force acts 1.5 m from a hinge at right angles. Torque?

children.note: Pick one sense as positive and keep it. Many textbooks and this library use anticlockwise = +.

children.topic: A force through the pivot has zero torque
children.note: Its lever arm is zero. This is the trick for choosing the pivot: put it where an unknown force acts, and that unknown disappears from the torque equation.

manas.q: Where should you put the pivot to make an unknown force vanish from the torque equation?

children.note: If forces sum to zero and torques about one point sum to zero, then torques about every other point sum to zero too — shifting the pivot adds R × ΣF, which is zero. So you choose the pivot for convenience.

manas.q: Why are we free to choose any pivot point in an equilibrium problem?

children.note: With the z-axis as the rotation axis the six equations shrink to ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, Στz = 0. Three unknowns at most can be found; more unknowns means the problem is statically indeterminate.

manas.q: How many independent equilibrium equations does a planar problem give?

children.topic: Centre of mass carries the weight
children.note: For torque purposes, a uniform beam's whole weight acts at its midpoint; a uniform plate's at its centre.
Find the centre of mass first (given, or by balancing). A loaded lorry or a crane with its boom out has it well away from the geometric middle.
OpenStax's problem-solving strategy for rigid bodies in equilibrium. Follow it in order every time; most mistakes come from skipping step 2.

manas.q: List the five steps for solving a static-equilibrium problem.

children.topic: 1 · Identify the body, the forces, the question
children.note: Which object? What acts on it? What is asked, and what is given — including facts hidden in the wording ("uniform beam" means weight at the centre).

children.topic: 2 · Draw the free-body diagram and pick a pivot
children.note: Axes, every force, components, labels. For an unknown force guess a direction; a negative answer later means it points the other way. Mark the pivot and the lever arms.

manas.q: What does a negative answer for an unknown force mean?

children.note: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, Στ = 0 about the chosen pivot, each force with its sign.
As many equations as unknowns. Keep symbols until the end; substitute numbers last.
Right unit (N or N·m)? Sensible size? Re-solve about a different pivot as an independent check.
Three problems, each recomputed step by step. Cover the answer and try first.

children.topic: A · Seesaw: where must the heavier child sit?
children.note: A 30 kg child sits 2.0 m left of the pivot. A 40 kg child sits on the right at distance d. Torques about the pivot: 30 × 9.8 × 2.0 = 40 × 9.8 × d, so d = 60/40 = 1.5 m. (g cancels.)

manas.q: 30 kg at 2.0 m balances 40 kg at what distance?

children.note: ΣFy = 0: the pivot pushes up with (30 + 40) × 9.8 = 686 N.

children.topic: B · Beam on two supports with a load
children.note: Uniform beam, 4.0 m, 20 kg (196 N at its middle, 2.0 m from A). A 60 kg load (588 N) sits 1.0 m from support A. Find the support reactions R_A and R_B.

manas.q: Set up the torque equation about A for the beam example.

children.note: R_B × 4.0 = 196 × 2.0 + 588 × 1.0 = 392 + 588 = 980 N·m, so R_B = 245 N. R_A drops out because it acts at A.
R_A + R_B = 196 + 588 = 784 N, so R_A = 784 − 245 = 539 N. The support nearer the load carries more — as expected.

manas.q: In the beam example, why does R_A carry more than R_B?

children.note: R_A × 4.0 = 196 × 2.0 + 588 × 3.0 = 392 + 1764 = 2156 N·m, so R_A = 539 N. Same answer from a different pivot: solved.
A 1000 L tank (1000 kg of water, 9800 N) plus a 200 kg tank-and-frame (1960 N) stands on four equal legs. Symmetry: each leg carries 11 760 / 4 = 2940 N. Each leg's footing must take about 3 kN.

manas.q: A full 1000 L tank on a 200 kg stand with four legs: load per leg?

children.note: Symmetry breaks; use torques about one pair of legs to find how the load shifts — the legs under the heavy side carry more. This is why stands are levelled.
Each of these has been seen in first-year scripts — and in collapsed sheds.

children.topic: Drawing the net force or "ma" as a force
children.note: Only real pushes and pulls from other bodies go on the diagram: weight, normal, tension, friction. Why: ma is the result of those forces, not one more force — drawing it counts it twice. Check: name the body behind every arrow.

children.topic: Normal force drawn vertical on a slope
children.note: It is perpendicular to the surface, so it tilts with the slope. Why: the surface can only push straight out of itself. Example: a 10 kg box on a 30° ramp has N = mg cos 30° = 98 × 0.866 ≈ 85 N, not 98 N. Check: at 0° (flat) cos 0° = 1 and N = mg again.

children.topic: Both halves of an action–reaction pair on one body
children.note: They act on different bodies; only one belongs on any single diagram. Why: put both on one body and they cancel, so nothing could ever be pushed. Example: a book on a table — the table pushes up on the book (book's diagram); the book pushes down on the table (table's diagram).

children.topic: Using the full distance instead of the lever arm
children.note: Torque needs the perpendicular distance, or r F sin θ. Why: only the part of the force square to the arm turns it. Example: 50 N on a 0.30 m spanner at 30° to the handle gives 0.30 × 50 × sin 30° = 7.5 N·m, not 15 N·m. Check: push straight along the handle and the nut does not turn.

Decide the positive sense once; write every torque with that sign. Why: one flipped sign turns a balance into a sum and gives a reaction that is too big or negative. Example: in the 4 m beam, anticlockwise positive about A: R_B × 4.0 − 196 × 2.0 − 588 × 1.0 = 0 → R_B = 245 N. Check: a negative reaction means a sign slipped (or the support must pull down).
Three unknowns per planar body. A fourth needs another body's diagram or a deformation argument (second year).

"Uniform beam of 20 kg" is a force at the midpoint — it is part of the problem. Why: the beam pulls down on its supports like any load. Example: in the 4 m beam, the 196 N at 2.0 m is that weight; leave it out and R_B comes out 147 N instead of 245 N. Check: the reactions must add up to every weight, the beam's included.
Say the answer aloud; tap a bubble for the source page.

ΣF = 0 (no push left over, so it does not slide off) and Στ = 0 about any axis (no turn left over, so it does not spin). Why both: a ladder can have ΣF = 0 and still tip over if the torques do not cancel.

manas.q: State the two conditions for static equilibrium.

children.topic: Q2 · 80 kg person on a 2.0 m plank, 0.5 m from end A
children.note: Weight 784 N. About A: R_B × 2.0 = 784 × 0.5 → R_B = 196 N; R_A = 588 N (plank weight ignored).

manas.q: An 80 kg person stands 0.5 m from end A of a light 2.0 m plank. Reactions?

children.topic: Q3 · Why put the pivot at a hinge?
children.note: The unknown hinge force passes through the pivot and has zero torque, leaving one equation with one unknown.

manas.q: Why choose the hinge as the pivot?

children.topic: Q4 · Cable at 20° holding a 300 N sign, two cables
children.note: Only the upward parts hold the sign: 2T sin 20° = 300, so T = 300 / (2 × 0.342) = 439 N each. Why so big: a flat cable has a small upward part, so it must pull hard. Check: hanging straight down (90°) each would carry just 150 N.

manas.q: Two cables at 20° above horizontal hold a 300 N sign. Tension in each?

children.topic: Q5 · Is a car cruising at constant 80 km/h in equilibrium?
children.note: Yes — dynamic equilibrium: no acceleration, forces and torques balance.

manas.q: Is a car at a steady 80 km/h on a straight road in equilibrium?

children.note: Isolate the body, draw every real force, write ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0 about a pivot that kills an unknown, solve, then check with another pivot. The free-body diagram is the whole skill; the algebra is routine.
Previous map: Units, dimensions and estimation (N and N·m). Coming next in this library: Dynamics (Newton's second law), Materials (stress and strain — what the 3 kN per leg does to the steel).

children.topic: The three laws in one line each
children.note: Newton's laws link forces to motion. First: no net force, no change in motion. Second: net force = mass × acceleration. Third: forces come in equal and opposite pairs on two different bodies.

manas.q: State Newton's three laws in one line each.

children.note: A body keeps its velocity (including zero) unless a net force acts. A passenger lurches forward when a matatu brakes because their body carries on at the old speed.

manas.q: Why do standing passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes?

children.note: ΣF = ma: add every force on the body as vectors to get the net force; the acceleration points the same way as that net force.
If A pushes B, B pushes A equally and oppositely. The two forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other on one diagram.
The laws hold in frames that are not accelerating (inertial frames). Inside a braking bus, the "forward push" you feel is not a real force — it is the bus slowing under you.
The law is a vector equation, so write it once for each axis: ΣFₓ = maₓ and ΣF_y = ma_y.

manas.q: Write Newton's second law in component form.

children.note: Only the sum of all forces decides acceleration. A car at a steady 80 km/h has a big engine force but zero net force, because drag and rolling resistance balance it.

manas.q: A car cruises at a steady speed. What is the net force on it?

children.note: 1 N is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². A 100 g apple weighs about 1 N.

manas.q: Define one newton in base units.

children.note: Same force, double the mass, half the acceleration. Mass is measured in kg and does not change from place to place.
The general law is ΣF = rate of change of momentum (p = mv). For a fixed mass this becomes ma. The momentum form handles rockets and conveyor belts that gain or lose mass.
A 2000 kg loaded matatu goes from 0 to 50 km/h (13.9 m/s) in 10 s. a = 13.9 ÷ 10 = 1.39 m/s². Net force = 2000 × 1.39 ≈ 2780 N.

manas.q: 2000 kg, 0 to 50 km/h in 10 s: acceleration and net force?

children.note: 2780 N is the net force. The tyres must push forward by 2780 N plus whatever drag and rolling resistance oppose the motion.
Mass is how much matter (kg). Weight is the gravitational pull on it (N): w = mg, with g = 9.8 m/s² near the Earth's surface.

manas.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?

children.note: Weight = 70 × 9.8 = 686 N. Bathroom scales show 70 "kg" because they divide the force by g.

manas.q: Weight of a 70 kg person?

children.note: Problems use g = 9.8 m/s². The real value differs a little from place to place on Earth — too little to matter in first-year work. Weight changes with g; mass does not.
Shops say "kilograms" for weight; engineers keep kg for mass and N for force. Writing "a force of 50 kg" in a script loses marks.
Almost every problem uses a few named forces. Each has a rule for its direction.
Always straight down toward the Earth's centre, acting at the centre of mass.
A surface pushes back at right angles to itself. It is not always equal to mg — it changes on slopes and in lifts.

manas.q: Is the normal force always equal to mg?

children.note: A rope or cable can only pull, along its own length. A light rope over a smooth pulley has the same tension on both sides.
Acts along the surface, opposing sliding (or the tendency to slide). Static up to μₛN; kinetic about μₖN.
Proportional to stretch or squeeze and opposite to it: F = −kx (Hooke's law), k in N/m.

manas.q: What is Hooke's law?

children.note: Air or water resistance, growing with speed. At highway speeds it is the main force the engine fights.

children.note: Five steps; the free-body diagram is where the marks are won.

manas.q: List the five steps for solving a Newton's-law problem.

children.note: Choose which object you will analyse. Choosing well can remove forces you do not know.
Every external force as an arrow from the body. Never draw "ma" as a force.
One axis along the acceleration if you know its direction (along a slope, up a lift shaft).

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.topic: 4 · Write ΣF = ma for each axis
children.note: Signs: forces along the positive axis are +, the others −. If the body does not accelerate on an axis, that sum is zero.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.note: Units in N, m/s², kg. Test extreme cases: if friction were zero, or the angle 90°, does the answer behave sensibly?

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.note: A 60 kg person stands on a scale in a lift. The scale reads the normal force N. Up is positive: N − mg = ma.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: What does a bathroom scale actually measure?

children.note: N = m(g + a) = 60 × 11.0 = 660 N. The scale shows 660 ÷ 9.8 = 67.3 "kg" — you feel heavier.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: 60 kg person, lift accelerating up at 1.2 m/s²: scale reading in N?

children.note: a = 0, so N = mg = 588 N; the scale shows 60 "kg". Speed alone does not change the reading.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: Lift moving up at constant speed: does the scale read more?

children.note: N = m(g − a) = 60 × 8.6 = 516 N, shown as 52.7 "kg" — you feel lighter.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.note: An 800 kg car accelerating up at 1.0 m/s² needs T = 800 × (9.8 + 1.0) = 8640 N. Real lifts add a large safety factor; check the current standard before any design.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.note: Bodies tied together share one acceleration. Solve the whole system first for a, then one body for the tension.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: How do you find the tension between two connected blocks?

children.topic: Two blocks pulled on a smooth table
children.note: 4 kg and 6 kg joined by a string; 20 N pulls the 6 kg block. Whole system: a = 20 ÷ 10 = 2.0 m/s². The string is the only force on the 4 kg block: T = 4 × 2.0 = 8.0 N.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: 4 kg and 6 kg tied together, 20 N pull on the 6 kg: acceleration and string tension?

children.note: On the 6 kg block: 20 − T = 6 × 2.0 = 12, so T = 8.0 N. Same answer.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.note: 5 kg and 3 kg hang over a smooth pulley. a = (5 − 3) ÷ (5 + 3) × 9.8 = 2.45 m/s². Tension T = 2 × 5 × 3 × 9.8 ÷ 8 = 36.8 N.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: Atwood machine with 5 kg and 3 kg: acceleration?

children.note: T lies between the two weights (29.4 N and 49 N). If the masses were equal, a = 0 and T = mg.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.note: A 1200 kg car is towed with a = 0.50 m/s² against 300 N of rolling resistance. Rope tension = 1200 × 0.50 + 300 = 900 N.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: Towing 1200 kg at 0.50 m/s² against 300 N resistance: rope tension?

children.note: Static friction holds things still up to a limit; once sliding, kinetic friction is usually smaller. That is why a stuck box suddenly "breaks free".

manas.q: Why is it harder to start a box sliding than to keep it sliding?

children.note: Approximate values: rubber on dry concrete μₛ 1.0, μₖ 0.7; on wet concrete μₖ 0.3–0.5; wood on wood 0.5 / 0.3; steel on steel (dry) 0.6 / 0.3. Real values vary with surface and wear.
Wood on wood: N = 490 N. To start: 0.5 × 490 = 245 N. To keep sliding: 0.3 × 490 = 147 N. A 200 N push does not move it (friction matches 200 N).

manas.q: 50 kg crate, μₛ = 0.5, μₖ = 0.3: force to start it moving?

children.note: Once sliding, only kinetic friction (147 N) pushes back. a = (300 − 147) ÷ 50 = 3.06 m/s². Why: only the net force speeds the crate up — the 147 N lost to friction turns into heat, not speed. Check: the same 300 N on ice (almost no friction) would give 300 ÷ 50 = 6 m/s².
Block on a 30° slope with μₖ = 0.3: a = g(sin 30° − 0.3 cos 30°) = 2.35 m/s². Mass cancels — heavy and light blocks slide alike.

manas.q: Block sliding down 30° with μₖ = 0.3: acceleration?

children.note: A crate rides on a lorry only by static friction. The most the lorry can accelerate without it sliding is μₛg; with μₛ = 0.5 that is 4.9 m/s². Why loads must be strapped.

manas.q: Crate on a lorry bed, μₛ = 0.5: maximum acceleration before it slides?

children.note: Car at 72 km/h (20 m/s), locked wheels, rubber on dry concrete μₖ 0.7: a = 6.86 m/s², distance = v² ÷ 2a = 29 m. On wet road with μₖ 0.4: 51 m.

manas.q: 20 m/s, μₖ = 0.7: braking distance after the wheels lock?

children.note: Reaction time (about a second at 20 m/s adds 20 m), ABS keeping tyres at static grip, worn tyres and slopes. A road-safety figure, not a design value.
Distance grows with v². Twice the speed, four times the braking distance.

manas.q: If speed doubles, what happens to braking distance?

children.note: Every force has a partner on another body. Finding the partner tells you which body to draw.
Your foot pushes the ground backward; the ground pushes you forward (friction). Tyres do the same — on mud, the push fails and the wheels spin.

manas.q: What force pushes a car forward?

children.note: "If the cart pulls back on the donkey equally, how can they move?" Because the two forces act on different bodies. The donkey moves forward because the ground pushes it harder than the cart pulls back.

children.topic: Weight and normal force are NOT a pair
children.note: Both act on the same body. The partner of your weight is your pull on the Earth; the partner of the normal force is your push on the floor.

manas.q: Are weight and the normal force a third-law pair?

children.note: Once you know a, the constant-acceleration equations give speeds, times and distances.

children.note: The three equations assume a never changes. Why it is usually fine: constant forces give constant a, and many real motions are close to that. When it is not (air drag growing with speed, a spring) use small time steps or calculus.

manas.q: When are v = u + at and its partners NOT valid?

children.topic: Pick the equation with one unknown
children.note: List what you know (u, v, a, s, t). Choose the equation that contains the one you want and leaves out the one you neither know nor need. Stopping distance with no time given → v² = u² + 2as.

children.topic: Worked: braking from 90 km/h, dry and wet
children.note: 90 km/h = 25 m/s. Braking at 7.0 m/s² (dry): s = 25² ÷ (2 × 7.0) ≈ 45 m. At 5.0 m/s² (wet): 25² ÷ 10 ≈ 63 m. Same car, same speed — the road adds 18 m. (Deceleration values as in the OpenStax example; real ones vary with tyres and road.)

manas.q: Stopping distance from 25 m/s at 7.0 m/s²?

children.note: Before the brakes bite the car keeps its full speed for the reaction time. Allow 1.0 s at 25 m/s: 25 m more, so about 70 m in all on a dry road. Why it matters: tiredness or a phone lengthens the reaction time, and this part grows with speed, not speed squared.

manas.q: Why add a reaction-time distance to the braking distance?

children.topic: Worked: catching up from a stop
children.note: A boda boda passes a waiting car at a steady 10 m/s; the car starts at that moment with 1.0 m/s². Same position when 10t = ½ × 1.0 × t² → t = 20 s, 200 m on. The car is then at 20 m/s (72 km/h). Set the two positions equal — that is the whole method.

manas.q: How do you find when a chasing vehicle catches up?

children.topic: Free fall: the same a for every mass
children.note: With air resistance negligible, everything near the Earth falls with the same acceleration g, whatever its mass — a hammer and a feather on the Moon showed it in 1971. g varies from about 9.78 to 9.83 m/s² with place; we use 9.8.

manas.q: Does a heavier object fall faster when air resistance is negligible?

children.topic: Worked: a spanner dropped from 20 m
children.note: h = ½gt² → t = √(2 × 20 ÷ 9.8) ≈ 2.0 s. It lands at v = gt ≈ 20 m/s, about 71 km/h. This is why sites insist on hard hats, toe boards and tool lanyards.

manas.q: A tool falls 20 m. Roughly how fast does it land?

children.topic: Choose a sign and keep it
children.note: Pick up (or down) as positive at the start and never switch. With up positive, a = −9.8 m/s² for a falling or rising object. Check: a ball thrown up has v = 0 at the top, but a is still −9.8 m/s².

manas.q: At the top of its flight, what is a thrown ball's acceleration?

children.note: ma is the result of the forces, not one of them. Why: F = ma says the forces add up to ma; drawing ma as an extra arrow counts the same effect twice. Example: a 2 kg trolley pulled with 10 N on smooth ground has one horizontal arrow (10 N) and a = 5 m/s²; add an "ma" arrow and the sum becomes 20 N, which is wrong.

Only true on level ground with no vertical acceleration and no slanted pull. Work it out from ΣF_y each time. Example: pull a 10 kg box with 50 N at 30° above level. The pull lifts it by 50 × sin 30° = 25 N, so N = 98 − 25 = 73 N, not 98 N — and the friction gets smaller with it.

Force in N. Multiply by g to turn mass into weight. Why: kg measures how much matter there is; N measures a push or pull. Example: a 50 kg sack weighs 50 × 9.8 = 490 N, not "50" — put 50 into ΣF = ma as a force and every answer is about 10 times too small.

children.topic: Forgetting friction can be less than μₛN
children.note: μₛN is the maximum. A box that is not moving has exactly as much friction as needed to balance the push. Why: static friction only reacts to what tries to slide the box; it never pushes harder than that. Example: a 10 kg box with μₛ = 0.5 can hold up to 0.5 × 98 = 49 N. Push it with 20 N and it stays put with 20 N of friction, not 49 N. Check: 49 N against a 20 N push would make the box slide back towards you.

manas.q: Is static friction always equal to μₛN?

children.note: They act on different bodies and never appear on the same diagram. Why: each force of the pair pushes a different body, so they cannot cancel. Example: the cart pulls the horse back as hard as the horse pulls it forward, yet both move — the ground pushes the horse's hooves forward harder than the cart pulls back. Check: label every arrow "on whom, by whom"; a pair swaps the two names.

Divide km/h by 3.6 before using F = ma or the motion equations. Why: the equations assume metres and seconds, and 1 km/h is only 1/3.6 m/s. Example: a car braking from 54 km/h in 5 s: 54 ÷ 3.6 = 15 m/s, so a = 3 m/s²; using 54 directly gives 10.8 m/s², more than g — a sign something is wrong.

children.topic: Q5 · Why does a heavy lorry need longer to stop?
children.note: In the simple model it does not: a = μg, whatever the mass. In real life lorry brakes heat up and fade, and tyres cannot use their full grip without skidding, so heavy vehicles do take longer.
